en: The Hymn to Śiva’s Tāṇḍava Dance Composed by Rāvaṇa

My delight at every moment is fixed upon Him who bears the crescent moon as His crest-jewel, whose head is resplendent with the creeper-like waves of the flowing Nila-nirjhari river tossing about within the cavity of His matted locks, and upon the fire blazing "dhag-dhag-dhag" on the expanse of His forehead.

May my mind find delight in that certain Reality within the sky of consciousness— that which gladdens the hearts of those whose minds rejoice in the continuous expansion of the quarters, made beautiful by its kinship with the playful grace of the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, and which wards off insurmountable calamities with a torrent of compassionate glances.

May the Lord of Beings bring wonderful delight to the mind—He whose face is the horizon, anointed with the saffron paste of the mass of radiance from the jewels on the throbbing hoods of the serpents in His matted locks; He who is radiant with the upper garment of the shimmering hide of an elephant blinded by rut.

May the one who has the friend of the cakora birds as his crest-jewel long bring about prosperity—he whose footstool is greyed by the showers of pollen from the flowers crowning the heads of all the gods beginning with the thousand-eyed Indra; whose mass of matted locks is bound with the serpent-king’s coil;
and who, bowing to the lord of the immortals, wears the five arrows of the God of Love that appear like sparks from the blazing fire of the forehead’s marketplace.
May the matted-haired head of the Great Skull-Bearer, its crest resplendent with a streak of nectar-rays, be for our supreme prosperity!

May my mind be fixed on the Three-Eyed One, who—by means of the fire blazing with a "dhag-dhag" roar upon his formidable forehead-slate—has surpassed the fierce five-arrowed god of love; and who is the sole master artisan in crafting the variegated leaf-designs upon the breasts of the Mountain King’s daughter.

May the elephant of poetic composition—the sustainer of the world, beautiful as the moon, and the bearer of the mountain-like streams of the gods—bestow prosperity upon us; he whose neck is like the stalk of a bandhūka flower amidst the dense mass of darkness of the kuhū night, which is otherwise difficult to endure and obstructed by a circle of fresh clouds.

May he, whose neck possesses a continuous luster that mocks the dark splendor of a multitude of blooming blue lotuses, grant us fortune. 7. May the elephant of poetic composition—the sustainer of the world, beautiful as the moon, and the bearer of the mountain-like streams of the gods—bestow prosperity upon us; he whose neck is like the stalk of a bandhūka flower amidst the dense mass of darkness of the kuhū night, which is otherwise difficult to endure and obstructed by a circle of fresh clouds. May he, whose neck possesses a continuous luster that mocks the dark splendor of a multitude of blooming blue lotuses, grant us fortune.

I worship Him who cuts through passion, who cuts through the [three] cities, who cuts through worldly existence, who cut through the sacrifice, who cut through the elephant [Gajasura], who cut through Andhaka, and who cut through Death himself.

I worship Him, the ender of Death— the destroyer of Smara, the destroyer of Pura, the destroyer of Bhava, the destroyer of Makha, the destroyer of Gaja, and the destroyer of Andhaka— who acts as a honeybee for the blossoming sweetness of the flowing nectar from the clusters of Kadamba flowers that are the digits of all auspiciousness free from pride.

May Śiva be victorious— he whose fierce *tāṇḍava* dance is set in motion by the succession of lofty, auspicious sounds from drums resounding "dhim-dhim-dhim," and whose terrifying firebrand-spear flashes with the hissing hiss of serpents whirling in their unceasing gyrations.

When shall I worship Sadāśiva, making my mind regard as equal: a bed variegated with flowers and one covered in gravel; a necklace of serpent-pearls and a string of precious gems and a clod of earth; a friend and an enemy faction; a blade of grass and the lotus-eyed Goddess; and the subjects and the great king of the earth?

When, dwelling in the hollow of a bower by a stream of the celestial river, freed from all evil thoughts and always bearing my joined palms to my head; when, with my forehead adorned by the tremulous eyes of Rāvaṇa as he performs the Śiva-tāṇḍava dance, I utter the mantra "Śiva"—when shall I become happy? 12
For by constantly reciting, remembering, and speaking this supreme of all praises, which has been thus declared, a person attains perpetual purity.
He quickly gains devotion toward Hari and his Guru; otherwise, there is no other path, for the contemplation of Śaṅkara alone brings liberation to embodied beings.
(13) Whoever recites at the conclusion of worship, during the evening twilight, this adoration of Śambhu sung by the Ten-faced One—
Śambhu ever bestows upon him a stable and auspicious fortune, accompanied by chariots, lordly elephants, and horses.
(14) Thus ends the Śivatāṇḍava Stotra composed by the illustrious Rāvaṇa.
